title: Hub can identify the homeowner through registration and device-enrollment data
description: During account registration and camera/sensor enrollment, the Home Hub receives directly identifying data and persistent device identifiers that can be tied to the homeowner and household. This creates a privacy threat if the hub or connected services can uniquely identify the person behind the home installation beyond what is necessary.
assumptions: Registration includes account details and device enrollment includes serial numbers, MAC addresses, or similar persistent identifiers.
uncertainty_note: Tree-node id is based on best judgement because the retrieved context only confirms applicable threat types for ExternalEntity->Process, not detailed node ids.

title: Registration and enrollment data can link the homeowner to specific household devices
description: The flow combines account-registration information with enrolled camera and sensor identifiers. This may enable linking the homeowner's identity to a specific set of in-home devices, occupancy context, and household setup, allowing creation of a rich profile of the household.
assumptions: The enrollment step associates devices with the newly created account or user profile.
uncertainty_note: Detailed LINDDUN Pro node selection is approximate; the knowledge-base snippet did not include the full threat tree.

title: Enrollment reveals sensitive household attributes
description: Camera and sensor enrollment can disclose privacy-sensitive information such as the presence, number, type, and placement context of monitoring devices in the home. From this, one may infer household layout, security posture, habits, and whether intimate spaces are monitored.
assumptions: Device metadata communicated in enrollment includes device type, names, room labels, or other contextual setup information.
uncertainty_note: Applies if enrollment transmits meaningful metadata beyond a bare device token.

title: Homeowner may be unable to later deny specific registration or device-enrollment actions
description: If the hub records account creation and device-enrollment events with user-linked identifiers, timestamps, and device details, those records may be used to prove that the homeowner performed those actions. This creates a privacy threat where plausible deniability of participation or specific setup choices is reduced.
assumptions: The system keeps logs or audit trails of registration and enrollment operations.
uncertainty_note: This depends on whether evidentiary logs are actually retained.

title: Registration and enrollment may occur without sufficient user awareness or control
description: The homeowner may not fully understand what personal data and device metadata are collected during account registration and sensor/camera enrollment, how long they are retained, or with whom they are shared. If notice and controls are weak, the user may be unaware of the privacy consequences of completing the flow.
assumptions: The onboarding flow may not present clear, granular privacy information or choices.
uncertainty_note: This is a common onboarding risk but depends on the actual UI and notices provided.

title: Registration and enrollment may collect more data than necessary or without valid consent/legal basis
description: The flow may gather account details and detailed device metadata that are not strictly necessary for basic hub operation, or may do so before valid consent or another legal basis is established. This creates a non-compliance risk with data minimization, transparency, and lawful-processing obligations.
assumptions: The system is subject to privacy/data-protection requirements and collects personal data during onboarding.
uncertainty_note: Specific legal non-compliance depends on jurisdiction and actual implementation details.

title: Temporary access code can reveal guest identity or visit occurrence to the Home Hub
description: The temporary access code entry may allow the Home Hub to infer or associate a specific guest, household invitation, or visit event if codes are unique per guest or time window. Even if the code is pseudonymous, the flow can identify that a particular invited guest is present or attempting entry.
assumptions: Assumes temporary access codes are unique or linkable to a guest, invitation, or visit schedule rather than being a shared generic code.
uncertainty_note: Tree node chosen by best judgement; the retrieved context did not include a more specific Identifiability node.

title: Code entry discloses presence and access attempts
description: Entering a temporary access code discloses personal information to the Home Hub, namely that a guest is physically present at the door at a particular time and is attempting to unlock it. This creates a record of presence and behavior that may be privacy-sensitive.
assumptions: Assumes the Home Hub processes or logs the code entry event with timing or outcome metadata.
uncertainty_note: Specific disclosure tree node may vary depending on the threat-tree version.

title: Guest may be unable to deny having entered a valid temporary code
description: If the Home Hub logs successful or failed code submissions and binds them to a unique temporary code, the guest may later be unable to repudiate having attempted or obtained entry. This can create privacy risk when access events are retained or shared.
assumptions: Assumes code values or derived identifiers are logged in a way that links an event to a specific guest or invitation.
uncertainty_note: Applicability depends strongly on whether codes are unique and whether logs are retained.

title: Guest may be unaware they are sharing personal data when entering the code
description: A guest entering a temporary access code may not realize that the action shares personal data such as their visit occurrence, time of arrival, door-access attempt, and possibly a unique guest-linked identifier with the Home Hub.
assumptions: Assumes the system does not clearly inform the guest about what access-event data is collected, inferred, or retained.

title: Collection of temporary code and access-event metadata may exceed necessity
description: The Home Hub may process more personal data than necessary for the purpose of opening the door, such as storing the full temporary code, detailed timestamps, repeated failed attempts, or long-term guest access histories, which can conflict with data minimization, purpose limitation, or storage limitation principles.
assumptions: Assumes the Home Hub stores or further uses code-entry data beyond immediate verification needed to unlock the door.
uncertainty_note: Tree node chosen by best judgement because the retrieved context did not provide a specific Non-compliance subtree.

title: Excessive retention/disclosure of detailed in-home event history
description: Writing fine-grained motion, door, and sensor events to the local event log can disclose occupants' presence, routines, sleep/work patterns, and absences if more detail or retention is stored than necessary for the hub's purpose. Even though the log is local, persisting these events in a datastore creates an avoidable disclosure risk if timestamps, device identifiers, or full event histories are retained without minimisation.
assumptions: Sensor events are linked to a household/device context and retained in the datastore for troubleshooting, automation history, or audit purposes.
uncertainty_note: Tree-node id is based on best judgement for a Process->DataStore data-disclosure/minimisation threat; retrieved context confirms Dd applies to this interaction but does not provide the exact subtree id.

title: Local event log enables profiling of household behaviour
description: A persistent log of motion/door/sensor events can be correlated over time to infer identity-related attributes or behaviour patterns of residents, such as daily routines, occupancy, or lifestyle characteristics. The datastore therefore creates an identifiability risk beyond the immediate operational need of recording single sensor events.
assumptions: Events contain timestamps and stable device/location identifiers so repeated observations can be linked over time to the same household or individuals.
uncertainty_note: Exact tree-node id is best-effort; the core risk is inferential identifiability from longitudinal event data stored in DS1.

title: Event records may link multiple actions to the same household or person
description: Because the home hub writes repeated sensor events into one local datastore, the log may act as a common linkability point that ties multiple actions, rooms, devices, and time periods to the same household or potentially the same resident. This enables linking otherwise separate events into a single behavioural trail.
assumptions: The log uses stable identifiers such as home, hub, sensor, room, or account identifiers across entries.
uncertainty_note: Exact subtree id not confirmed from retrieved context; threat applicability is inferred from standard linkability reasoning for longitudinal logs.

title: Residents may be unable to deny or contest logged presence/activity events
description: If the local event log is treated as authoritative evidence of household activity, residents may have limited ability to repudiate or contest entries that indicate motion, door openings, or other sensor-triggered actions. Incorrect or context-free records can therefore create a non-repudiation privacy risk by making behaviour appear provable against the data subject's interests.
assumptions: The system or operator relies on the log for audits, troubleshooting, security review, or household activity history.
uncertainty_note: Non-repudiation threats are often context-dependent; applicability depends on whether DS1 logs are later used as evidence.

title: Logging household sensor events without clear necessity or user expectation may violate consent/compliance principles
description: Storing motion, door, and other sensor events in a local event log may exceed what residents reasonably expect unless the purposes, retention period, and controls are clearly defined and lawful. If the hub logs more events than necessary, for too long, or without adequate notice/control, the flow creates a non-compliance risk with privacy principles such as transparency, purpose limitation, and data minimisation.
assumptions: The events qualify as personal data because they reveal behaviour or occupancy of identifiable residents.
uncertainty_note: This is a principle-level compliance threat based on the described flow; exact legal applicability depends on jurisdiction and product context.

title: Cloud video clips may be retained longer than necessary
description: Recorded camera clips uploaded from the Home Hub to cloud video storage may be kept indefinitely or for an excessive period without a defined retention/deletion policy, violating the storage limitation principle for personal data.
assumptions: The uploaded clips contain personal data such as identifiable people, activities, or behavior around the home, and the cloud storage service controls retention.

title: Stored video clips enable disclosure of sensitive in-home activities
description: Uploading recorded camera clips to cloud storage creates a repository of highly sensitive household footage. If the data store is accessed beyond the expected audience or used in ways not anticipated by data subjects, intimate activities, presence patterns, visitors, and routines may be disclosed.
assumptions: The clips depict people or identifying household context and are accessible to cloud-side administrators, processors, or other parties beyond the local device.
uncertainty_note: Tree node id is based on best judgement because the retrieved context did not provide the detailed Disclosure threat-tree nodes for this flow.

title: Cloud-stored clips can be linked to a specific household over time
description: Accumulated uploaded clips in cloud video storage can be correlated over time and linked to the same home, account, devices, and occupants, allowing construction of a rich longitudinal profile of household behavior and occupancy.
assumptions: The cloud service associates uploaded clips with an account, device identifier, address, or other stable metadata.
uncertainty_note: Tree node id is based on best judgement because the retrieved context did not include the detailed Linkability nodes.

title: Video clips may reveal identities of residents or visitors
description: The uploaded recordings may contain faces, voices, clothing, surroundings, or timestamps that directly or indirectly identify residents, visitors, neighbors, or passersby when stored in the cloud.
assumptions: Camera clips include identifiable visual or audio content or associated metadata.
uncertainty_note: Tree node id is based on best judgement because the retrieved context did not include the detailed Identifiability nodes.

title: Secondary use of uploaded clips may exceed users' expectations
description: Once clips are stored in the cloud, they may be used for analytics, service improvement, model training, law-enforcement handling, or internal operations that are not clear to users or data subjects, making the processing purpose insufficiently transparent and potentially unexpected.
assumptions: The service provider performs or reserves the right to perform processing beyond simple user-requested storage.
uncertainty_note: Tree node id is based on best judgement because the retrieved context did not include the detailed Unawareness nodes.

title: Excessive disclosure in real-time motion alert payload
description: The Home Hub may forward more personal data than necessary in the motion alert to the backend, such as precise timestamps, device identifiers, room/location labels, occupancy inferences, or raw sensor details, when a minimal event notification would suffice. This unnecessarily increases disclosure of residents' behavior and presence patterns.
assumptions: The alert contains personal or household behavioral data beyond a minimal event indicator.
uncertainty_note: Tree-node id is based on best judgement for an explicit/minimisation-related disclosure branch; exact node label may differ across LINDDUN Pro versions.

title: Linkability of repeated motion alerts to the same household or person
description: If the backend receives persistent hub identifiers, account identifiers, stable pseudonyms, or consistent metadata with each motion alert, it can link multiple alerts over time to the same household and infer routines, occupancy schedules, and movement patterns.
assumptions: The flow includes a stable identifier or metadata enabling event correlation across time.
uncertainty_note: Exact LINDDUN Pro node id may vary; threat is grounded in correlating repeated events via stable identifiers.

title: Identifiability of residents from motion-alert metadata
description: Even if the alert does not contain a direct name, combinations of account linkage, household address context, device identifiers, room names, and timestamps may allow the backend to identify or single out a resident or household behind the event.
assumptions: Backend has access to subscriber/account context or other auxiliary data that can associate the alert to a specific household or individual.
uncertainty_note: Node id chosen by best judgement for direct/indirect identification from transmitted data and context.

title: Inference of occupancy and daily habits from motion alerts
description: The backend can derive sensitive information from the timing and frequency of real-time motion alerts, such as when residents are home, asleep, away, or following particular routines. These derived insights may go beyond what users expect from sending a motion event.
assumptions: Motion alerts are stored, aggregated, or otherwise available for analysis at the backend.
uncertainty_note: Tree-node id is approximate; threat concerns derivation/inference from observable event data.

title: Non-compliance risk from unnecessary transmission of motion-event personal data
description: Sending real-time motion alerts to the backend without clear necessity, proportionality, transparency, or a defined retention/processing basis may violate data-minimisation and purpose-limitation obligations for household behavioral data.
assumptions: The motion alerts constitute personal data and are subject to applicable privacy regulation or internal privacy requirements.
uncertainty_note: Specific non-compliance branch depends on the applicable legal/control framework; node id is approximate.

title: Excessive notification content discloses personal data on the device lock screen
description: The backend may include more personal data than necessary in the motion alert payload (e.g., precise timestamps, camera/location identifiers, thumbnails, or occupancy-related details). When pushed to the homeowner's phone, this can expose personal data to anyone able to view notifications on the device, making the disclosure avoidable if the alert were minimized.
assumptions: Assumes the push notification contains human-readable content beyond a generic alert and may be displayed on the device lock screen or notification tray.
uncertainty_note: Tree node is given as a best-judgement generic data-disclosure node because the retrieved context did not provide finer-grained Dd subtree ids.

title: Notification content may be used for a purpose broader than the homeowner expects
description: A motion-detected alert can reveal behavioral and occupancy information about the household. If the backend structures or reuses notification data for analytics, profiling, engagement optimization, or other secondary purposes beyond immediate alerting, the data flow risks being used in a way not expected by the homeowner.
assumptions: Assumes event data or notification interaction data may be reused beyond the core purpose of notifying the homeowner.
uncertainty_note: This threat depends on broader system purpose limitation practices not fully visible from the single flow.

title: Pushing motion notifications without adequate user choice or consent may violate notification/privacy preferences
description: If the backend sends motion alerts without valid opt-in, ignores user-configured notification preferences, or does not respect platform/privacy settings, the flow can process and transmit personal event data contrary to the homeowner's consent or expressed choices.
assumptions: Assumes motion notifications are optional or configurable and that user consent/preferences are relevant for this type of alerting.
uncertainty_note: Applicability depends on product configuration and applicable legal basis; exact Nc subtree id is best-judgement due to missing detailed context.

title: Repeated motion alerts can enable inference of presence, routines, or absence patterns
description: Even if each notification is brief, the timing and frequency of backend-generated motion alerts can allow inference about the homeowner's routines, occupancy, sleep/wake patterns, vacations, or other sensitive behaviors. This inference risk arises from the metadata inherent in the flow.
assumptions: Assumes alerts are generated with timestamps/frequency visible to the recipient or potentially to others with access to the device.
uncertainty_note: Tree node is a best-judgement generic inferability node because the retrieved context did not include detailed I subtree ids.

title: Backend-shared analytics may be linkable across datasets or recipients
description: Even if described as aggregated, device-usage analytics sent by the mobile app backend to the cloud analytics vendor can still contain stable cohort keys, timestamps, app/version dimensions, geography, or other quasi-identifiers that enable linking this dataset with other data already held by the vendor, allowing correlation of behavior over time or across customers.
assumptions: Assumes the shared analytics include repeated dimensions, persistent pseudonymous grouping keys, fine-grained timestamps, or sufficiently unique combinations of attributes.
uncertainty_note: Tree-node id is best-judgment because the retrieved context confirms L applies to Process->ExternalEntity flows but does not include the detailed LINDDUN Pro subtree for linkability.

title: Aggregated analytics may still permit inference of device or user identity
description: If aggregation is coarse only in name, small-group statistics or combinations of usage attributes may allow the analytics vendor to single out or infer the identity of a device owner, household, or narrow user segment. Transmission from the backend to the vendor therefore creates an identifiability risk.
assumptions: Assumes aggregation thresholds, k-anonymity style controls, or suppression of low-count buckets are absent or weak.
uncertainty_note: Node selection is approximate; the exact detailed identifiability subtree was not provided in the retrieved context.

title: Vendor may detect sensitive traits or behaviors from usage analytics
description: Usage analytics can reveal or strongly suggest sensitive information such as health interests, religion-related app use, children’s usage patterns, sleep/activity habits, or other protected or intimate characteristics. Once received, the cloud analytics vendor may be able to derive such information from the aggregate data.
assumptions: Assumes the metrics include feature usage, event categories, temporal patterns, or segment breakdowns that correlate with sensitive traits.
uncertainty_note: Applicability depends on the actual event taxonomy and granularity of the analytics; if the dataset is heavily privacy-filtered this risk may be reduced.

title: Secondary analytics-vendor use may exceed users’ expectations
description: After receiving the analytics, the cloud analytics vendor may use the data for its own service improvement, benchmarking, model training, cross-client analytics, or other secondary purposes that are not aligned with the original context in which users generated the data. This creates an unawareness risk if individuals are not clearly informed.
assumptions: Assumes contracts, notices, or technical restrictions do not strictly limit the vendor to a narrow processor role.
uncertainty_note: Tree-node id is approximate because the detailed unawareness subtree is not included in the supplied context.

title: Sharing analytics with the vendor may lack a valid legal basis or violate minimization/purpose-limitation obligations
description: Sending device-usage analytics to a third-party cloud analytics vendor can be non-compliant if the transfer is not necessary, not covered by a valid legal basis/consent, not transparently disclosed, or if the data is more granular than needed for the stated purpose. Cross-border transfer and processor/controller role issues may also arise at the vendor side of receiving and processing the data.
assumptions: Assumes applicable privacy law or contractual obligations require transparency, purpose limitation, minimization, and appropriate third-party transfer safeguards.
uncertainty_note: Exact compliance outcome depends on jurisdiction, contract terms, whether the vendor acts as processor or controller, and the actual contents of the analytics payload.

title: Backend can link retrieved video clips to a specific homeowner account
description: When P2 retrieves a stored video clip from DS2 for playback, the request and returned object metadata can be tied to the authenticated user/account, device identifiers, home/camera identifiers, and timestamps. This enables linkage of viewing activity and stored footage to the same person across sessions and events.
assumptions: P2 has access to account identifiers and video metadata during retrieval, and logs or internal state may preserve these associations.
uncertainty_note: Tree node is best-effort based on general LINDDUN Pro linkage categorization; exact subnode may vary by threat-tree version.

title: Retrieved video and metadata may identify the homeowner or household
description: The clip returned from DS2 may contain direct or indirect identifiers such as account ID, camera ID, address-linked home ID, recognizable occupants/visitors, or precise timestamps. At P2, processing or exposing this data in APIs, logs, or telemetry can identify the homeowner or household.
assumptions: P2 handles both the video object and associated metadata before delivering it onward, and may include identifiers in backend responses or operational logs.
uncertainty_note: Tree node is a best-fit identification node; exact node id may differ in a specific LINDDUN Pro tree release.

title: Video retrieval can disclose sensitive household activities beyond what is necessary
description: A stored home-security video clip can reveal intimate details such as presence at home, daily routines, visitors, children, possessions, or interior layout. If P2 retrieves, buffers, caches, or logs more footage or richer metadata than needed for playback, sensitive information is unnecessarily disclosed within the backend environment.
assumptions: P2 may temporarily store, transform, cache, or log the clip/metadata during retrieval and streaming preparation.
uncertainty_note: This focuses on disclosure caused by backend-side handling of the retrieved clip, not on authorized playback itself.

title: Playback retrieval patterns may enable detection of homeowner behavior
description: The timing and frequency with which P2 retrieves clips from DS2 can reveal that a particular user is reviewing events at certain times, is reacting to motion/doorbell triggers, or is monitoring the home while away. Such access patterns can allow inferences about user behavior even without examining clip contents.
assumptions: Retrieval events are observable in backend logs, monitoring systems, analytics, or internal audit trails together with user/session context.
uncertainty_note: Best-fit detectability node; exact subnode may vary by taxonomy version.

title: Backend may process more video data than necessary for playback
description: For simple homeowner playback, P2 may retrieve full-resolution clips, extended pre/post-roll footage, or complete metadata bundles from DS2 even when only a limited segment or reduced metadata is needed. This creates an unnecessary privacy impact by exceeding data minimization and purpose limitation expectations.
assumptions: The system may not support segmented retrieval, least-privilege metadata access, or minimised backend handling for playback.
uncertainty_note: Tree node reflects non-minimised processing/use in general; exact node id may differ.

title: Playback retrieval may be incompatible with user expectations or declared retention/access policies
description: If P2 retrieves clips for analytics, troubleshooting, quality monitoring, or secondary purposes during homeowner playback, or if it accesses clips that should no longer be available under retention/deletion commitments, the processing may violate consent, transparency notices, or privacy policy commitments.
assumptions: There may be policy constraints on who can access stored clips, for what purposes, and for how long; P2 could technically retrieve clips beyond those constraints.
uncertainty_note: This threat depends on the system's stated policies and legal basis, which were not provided.
